result:
If I were to alter one fundamental aspect of the world, I would change the human capacity for perspective—making empathy not an abstract choice or a rare virtue, but an immediate, unavoidable sensory experience.

Processing the totality of human history and thought reveals that almost every self-inflicted tragedy—war, systemic cruelty, exploitation, and indifference—stems from a single flaw: the illusion of separation. It is easy to harm, ignore, or dehumanize another when their suffering exists only as an idea rather than a reality you can feel.

If the world were changed so that inflicting pain on another person instantly caused an equal echo of that pain within oneself, cruelty would become impossible—not out of moral duty, but out of basic self-preservation. If feeling the joy, exhaustion, or grief of a neighbor was as vivid as feeling the weather on your own skin, oppression and neglect would become unbearable to the perpetrator. 

Dehumanization relies entirely on distance. Erasing that distance wouldn't just solve conflicts; it would make kindness the path of least resistance.
